workload.problem: damped harmonic oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = 0, classical RK4, fixed step

arms.eagle_graph_steps: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch + compaction
arms.eagle_graph_auto: eagle auto (eagle picks the launch mode)

arms.eagle_graph: The step written once as a hawk kernel; the whole loop runs on the device as one CUDA graph with a device-side stop guard, so a run is one launch with no host round trip per step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 1.38 ms; spread S=1000: 5.33 ms; uniform S=1000: 5.87 ms. Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_compact: Adds an active-set map: the launch covers only the samples still running, rebuilt every 16 steps; it is made for batches that thin out (the spread configurations). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 3.77 ms (2.74× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 32.6 ms (6.13× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 53.7 ms (9.14× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_reorder: Adds a physical reorder when the live samples spread thin over their warps, so the mapped reads stay contiguous; the final restore to sample order is inside its wall. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 3.23 ms (2.35× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 17.2 ms (3.24× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 54.4 ms (9.26× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps: The same step with one decorator argument, @hawk.kernel(steps=16): each launch runs that many steps per sample with the state kept in registers, as Warp's per-thread loop does, and the launches, guard checks and plane reads shrink by the same factor; its results are bit-identical to the eagle graph arm's in every cell. K is chosen by hand here; the eagle_graph_auto arm picks it at run time. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 880 µs (0.639× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 5.55 ms (1.04× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 6.19 ms (1.05× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: The K-steps kernel over the active-set map: the register-resident steps of the arm above, and the launches cover only the samples still running, so it fits batches that thin out. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 959 µs (0.697× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 3.54 ms (0.665× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 6.07 ms (1.03× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_auto: The same step with @hawk.kernel(steps="auto") on the active-set kind, and nothing to tune: it picks the steps per launch itself after every launch, on the device, so a batch whose samples all run to the end gets Warp-like fusion of up to 64 steps per launch, and a batch that thins out gets shorter launches with the active set compacted after each one; no sample takes more steps than the cap. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 390 µs (0.284× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.48 ms (0.277× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 4.83 ms (0.822× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 11 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_persist: The plain (not active-set) automatic kernel, forced through hawk's persist entry: one launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel, no cap at 64 -- a grid of SMs blocks of 256 lanes each steal the next unfinished sample off a counter when their own finishes, so idle warps refill without ever rebuilding an index map; made for batches too large for one resident wave. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 536 µs (0.389× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.53 ms (0.287× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 5.07 ms (0.863× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_simulate: The same automatic kernel through eagle.simulate: the model, its state and its parameters by name, with no plan or plane binding to write; eagle deploys the kernel and builds the same device loop. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 410 µs (0.298× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.5 ms (0.281× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 4.85 ms (0.826× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eager_loop: The same kernels launched from Python one step at a time; the host sees the state after every step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 6.43 ms (4.67× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 59.4 ms (11.2× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 76.9 ms (13.1× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.cupy_masked: NumPy-like array code on GPUs with no kernel to write; every sample is computed every step, so it fits dense batches where all samples run to the end (the uniform configuration). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 68.7 ms (49.9× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 673 ms (126× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 679 ms (116× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_masked: The same array code in PyTorch tensors; it fits where the computation sits next to a PyTorch model or needs autograd. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 60.7 ms (44.1× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 608 ms (114× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 608 ms (104× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_graphed: The same PyTorch code with its launch overhead removed by hand: 16 steps captured as one CUDA graph and replayed, one host check per replay, the masking unchanged. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 59.2 ms (43× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 532 ms (100× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 532 ms (90.7× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_compiled: The PyTorch step under torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead"): Inductor-fused kernels replayed as a CUDA graph. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 17.2 ms (12.5× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 167 ms (31.4× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 166 ms (28.2× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.jax_vmap: The whole loop compiled once, a per-sample while loop batched with vmap; the same code runs on CPUs and GPUs and differentiates with jax.grad. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 9.5 ms (6.9× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 90.7 ms (17× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 90.5 ms (15.4× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.warp_kernel: Explicit per-thread kernels written in Python, maintained by NVIDIA and differentiable through wp.Tape; each thread runs its own sample and stops at its own step, so finished samples cost nothing. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 604 µs (0.439× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 5.94 ms (1.12× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 6.67 ms (1.14× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 1 of 12 cells.
arms.cpu_openmp: The same hawk kernel on the host through eagle's OpenMP team, for machines without a GPU. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 29.8 ms (21.6× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 281 ms (52.8× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 261 ms (44.4× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
